Part A · Chapter A1

What a model is

A model is a rule with dials. A baseline tells you whether the rule is worth keeping.

A model turns inputs into a prediction, and its parameters are dials that change the prediction. Fitting adjusts the dials to match examples with answers (supervised learning). The lazy model's score is the first one to beat. Later chapters fit the dials (linear and logistic regression), grade the result and try trees and boosting.

The sharks are made up: records generated from published length-weight relationships, not field data.

You will need: functions and exponents, the mean and reading charts. The code blocks use a little NumPy.

A model is a rule with dials

Guess first. You want a spadenose shark's weight, but you have only its length L in cm. The equation weight = a × L3 gives an answer once a is chosen. For a 41 cm shark L3 = 68,921, and these sharks weigh a fraction of a kilogram. Should a be about 0.0000033, about 0.033 or about 3.3?

The equation above is a model, a rule that turns an input into a prediction. Its form is fixed: we use L3 to approximate a shark's volume (exponents in Part 0), because weight grows with volume. Here a is a parameter, a dial you can turn. At any setting of the dial the equation gives one predicted weight for any given input (a shark's length), so turning the dial can change the predictions for all inputs. The person building the model chooses the form and then sets the dial, usually by fitting, where an algorithm turns a until the predictions match the recorded weights well.

  1. Dots are made-up sharks, the teal curve is the prediction, and the grey lines are its misses. Turn the dial to 3.3 (the slider counts millionths) and the average miss, the mean length of the grey lines, falls to about 0.025 kg.
  2. Turn the dial up to 7 and the average miss becomes larger than that of the lazy model, the dashed line, which always predicts the average weight, 0.226 kg.
Dial a: 7.00 millionthsAverage miss of the rule: 0Average miss of the lazy model: 0

With the dial at 3.3 the model misses by about 0.025 kg on average, against 0.113 kg for the lazy model, so the guess is about 3.3 millionths, or 0.0000033.

How it works

Take Tag 3305, the coral circle in the figure, a 41.0 cm adult. With the dial at a = 0.0000033 (3.3 on the slider), a × L3 = 0.0000033 × 68,921 gives a predicted weight of 0.227 kg, where L3 = 413. The recorded weight is 0.228 kg, so this setting of the dial is close for this shark. The boxes under the plot work out the same arithmetic as you turn the dial.

\(\hat y\)“y hat”, the prediction: 0.227 kg=athe dial, set to 0.0000033×L3length cubed: 68,921

A good setting of the dial gives a small average miss, which is smallest near a = 3.3 and grows on both sides. Fitting uses all the recorded sharks together, because a setting taken from one shark would match that shark closely and the others less well. A dial describes one parameter, but a large model has millions of parameters, and an algorithm sets them.

Common belief. A model is a long list of rules, one per case.

Why it fails. Nobody wrote “a 41 cm spadenose weighs 0.227 kg”. The model has one dial, and any setting of it gives a prediction for lengths nobody recorded.

Better account. A person writes the form, and fitting turns the dial to match the recorded data, so new data can bring a new setting without rewriting the form.

Quick quiz

The dial is set to a = 0. What does the model predict for a 50 cm shark, and why?

It predicts 0 kg. The prediction is a times L3, and anything times zero is zero. The lazy model, which says 0.226 kg, would do better.

Which part of the model is turned by fitting to recorded data, the form a × L3 or the dial a?

The dial a, which is the parameter. A person chose the form, and fitting turns a. This is why the same form can be reused for milk sharks, with the dial at a different setting.

The lazy model

The lazy model ignores the length. It says the average weight, 0.226 kg, for all sharks. It is a very simple model, and the next sections use it as a yardstick. A model with the dial at zero predicts 0 kg for all sharks. That does worse than the lazy model. With the average miss as the score, the median weight would do slightly better than the average as a constant (0.109 kg against 0.113 kg), but the lazy model for a number says the average, the choice that goes with squared miss in the next chapters.

Symbols

\[ \hat y = f(\mathbf{x};\,\theta) \qquad\text{here}\qquad \hat y = a\,L^{3} \]

  • \(f\) is the model: the form of the rule. \(\mathbf{x}\) is the input (also called a feature), here the length \(L\) in cm.
  • \(\theta\) (theta) is short for all the parameters together. This model has one, \(\theta = (a)\).
  • \(\hat y\) (read "y hat") is the prediction. The true answer is \(y\). In this book a hat marks a model's guess.

A second worked example

The figure tests the dial on 268 sharks. Here is the test by hand on three records from the code block below. Cube the length, multiply by the dial (in millionths, as in the figure), and compare with the weight. The miss is the gap with its sign dropped.

length, cmlength cubedweight, kgguess at a = 3.3missguess at a = 7miss
29.224,8970.0660.0820.0160.1740.108
42.878,4030.2870.2590.0280.5490.262
51.3135,0060.4130.4460.0330.9450.532
average miss, kg0.0260.301

At 3.3 millionths the misses are small and similar. At 7 millionths the miss grows with the length, because a wrong dial multiplies the length cubed and the longest shark has the biggest cube.

Where the form breaks

The best dial still leaves an average miss of 0.025 kg. The exponent in these records is 2.92 (A2 measures it), so the cube is slightly too steep. For the 31 sharks of 50 cm or more, the rule at 3.3 millionths is too heavy by 0.032 kg on average. Moving the dial cannot repair a form that is a little wrong. The best dial also differs between species. For the 82 cm hammerhead Tag 5519, 82 cubed is 551,368, and times 3.3 millionths gives 1.82 kg against a recorded 2.610 kg. The dial that fits Tag 5519 alone is 4.7 millionths.

In practice

Choose the form from what you know about the problem, start with the simplest one, and count its parameters. Write the model as a function with the parameters as arguments, as the code below does. A common mistake is to fit a dial on one group and apply it to another, as with Tag 5519. Fitting is the usual way to set a parameter. A person can also set it by hand, as the slider does, or start from values that someone fitted earlier on other data. A dial describes one parameter, but a large model has millions of parameters, and an algorithm sets them.

In Python

import numpy as np

# 8 made-up spadenose records: length in cm, weight in kg
length = np.array([18.2, 29.2, 33.2, 36.5, 39.4, 42.8, 46.4, 51.3])
weight = np.array([0.018, 0.066, 0.128, 0.169, 0.167, 0.287, 0.297, 0.413])

def model(length, a):
    return a * length ** 3          # the form of the rule: weight = a * length^3

for a in [7e-6, 3.3e-6]:
    guess = model(length, a)
    print(f"a = {a:.1e}: average miss = {np.abs(guess - weight).mean():.3f} kg")

lazy = weight.mean()                 # the lazy model: always the average weight
print(f"lazy model says {lazy:.3f} kg: average miss = {np.abs(lazy - weight).mean():.3f} kg")
a = 7.0e-06: average miss = 0.236 kg
a = 3.3e-06: average miss = 0.020 kg
lazy model says 0.193 kg: average miss = 0.104 kg

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Parameters have units. The dial \(a\) here has units of kg per cm3. If the predictions are all about a thousand times too large or too small, look for grams mixed with kilograms.

Where this is used

Used in: the line \(\hat y = w x + b\) has two dials and is the model of A2. A neuron in B1 is the same idea with a bend added.

More questions

At the best dial the average miss is 0.025 kg. Can a further move of the dial lower it?

No. The average miss is smallest at the best dial, so any move raises it. To lower it you must change the form, for example by making the exponent a second dial, as A2 does.

Learning from examples with answers

Guess first. The table below lists made-up sharks by tag, species, length, weight, girth, depth, month and whether the shark is an adult. You want a model that names the species from the other columns. Which column is the answer, which would you give the model, and what changes if you want the weight instead?

In supervised learning we fit a model to examples that come with answers. An example is one row of the table, such as Tag 4127, a 44.0 cm juvenile bamboo shark. Its inputs \(\mathbf{x}\), also called features, are its measurements, and its label \(y\), also called the target, is the answer to the question we ask. The fitted model should predict \(y\) from \(\mathbf{x}\), including for sharks it has not seen. The type of label decides the task: a category (a species) gives classification, and a number (a weight) gives regression.

  1. Find Tag 4127 in the second row. The label column is outlined in coral and the input columns are navy. Choose a question with the buttons and watch the label of Tag 4127 and the task change.
  2. In the last row, a new shark, “?” marks a value its record lacks; for the species and adult questions that is the label, which a fitted model predicts. Untick “use” under a column to remove an input: with none left, a model can only say the same thing for all sharks.
Question
…kind of task
600 examplesthe full table has 600 rows
6 inputscounted from the ticked columns
…x of example 1: the inputs for Tag 3305→…y of example 1: its label

A different question gives Tag 4127 a different label, so one table can pose a classification task or a regression task.

How it works

Take Tag 4127 again. For the question “species” its label is “bamboo” and the task is classification. For the question “weight” its label is 0.281 kg and the task is regression. The label column differs because the question picks it, and that column cannot also be an input.

\(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\)inputs of example number i: d numbers, for Tag 4127 its measurements; the (i) numbers the examples and is not a power→\(y^{(i)}\)its label, the answer to the question\(i = 1,\dots,m\)m examples, here 600

The word “supervised” refers to the labels: someone or something supplied a recorded answer to the question (a scale reading, an expert's judgment), so fitting has answers to match. A useful input contains information about the label. The tag number 4127 contains none, because it is only a name, though a flexible model could memorise the tags it has seen.

Common belief. A trained model stores the table, rows like Tag 4127, and looks up the most similar shark.

Why it fails. The cube rule keeps one number, a, so the 268 spadenose records it was fitted on could be deleted, and it would still give a prediction for a new length.

Better account. The models in this primer keep fitted parameters and not the examples.

Quick quiz

To predict from length and girth whether a shark such as Tag 4127 is an adult, what is the label, and is this regression or classification?

The label is “adult or juvenile” (“juvenile” for Tag 4127). It has two possible values, so this is classification.

A table lists 768 women with glucose, BMI (body mass index), age and diabetes (yes or no). Which column is the label, what are \(m\) and \(d\), and what is the task?

The label is the yes or no column, with \(m = 768\) and \(d = 3\). The label is a category, so the task is classification.

Go deeper symbols, matrix form, clinic example, Python about 3 min

Symbols

\[ \bigl\{(\mathbf{x}^{(i)},\, y^{(i)})\bigr\}_{i=1}^{m} \qquad\text{with}\qquad \mathbf{x}^{(i)} = (x^{(i)}_1,\, \dots,\, x^{(i)}_d) \]

  • \(m\) is the number of examples, here 600 in the full table. \(i\) numbers them, so \(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\) is the inputs of the \(i\)-th shark and \(y^{(i)}\) its label.
  • \(d\) is the number of inputs for one shark. The subscript \(j\) in \(x_j\) numbers the inputs.
  • \(y\) is the label, also called the target.

From the table to a matrix

In code, the table becomes a matrix \(X\) with one row per shark and one column per input, and a vector \(\mathbf{y}\) with one label per shark.

An example from the clinic

The same layout fits the clinic story. The Pima data is a published dataset of 768 women of Pima heritage, measured in the United States, not data from Mumbai. Woman A is one row, and her label is the diagnosis:

(158, 31.6, 28)x of Woman A: glucose, BMI, age→1y: she has diabetesd = 3inputsm = 768women in the table

When it fails

Supervised learning works when the label depends on the inputs and the examples look like the cases you will meet later. It fails when labels are wrong, when the inputs lack the information, or when the future differs from the past. A label also costs effort: a weight needs a scale and a species needs an expert.

Methods that store examples

The models in this primer keep fitted parameters and not the examples. A few other methods do store examples, and this primer leaves them out.

In practice

Before you fit anything, count the rows and columns, and look for values that mean "not measured". The Pima file stores 374 missing insulin readings as 0, and a model fitted to them as if they were measurements learns nonsense. Ask who produced the label, and when (A4 covers leaks).

In Python

import numpy as np

# columns: length (cm), girth (cm). Rows: made-up Tags 4127, 3305, 5519 and 4766
X = np.array([[44.0, 12.4], [41.0, 11.5], [82.0, 27.6], [29.2, 7.3]])
y = np.array([0.281, 0.228, 2.610, 0.066])   # weight in kg: the label

m, d = X.shape
print("examples m =", m, " inputs d =", d)
print("example 1: x =", X[0], " y =", y[0])
examples m = 4  inputs d = 2
example 1: x = [44.  12.4]  y = 0.281
import numpy as np

# three made-up sharks (Tags 4127, 3305 and 5519): the inputs are length and depth
length = np.array([44.0, 41.0, 82.0])
depth = np.array([0.4, 18.0, 14.0])
species = np.array(["bamboo", "spadenose", "hammerhead"])
weight = np.array([0.281, 0.228, 2.610])

X = np.c_[length, depth]             # one row per shark, one column per input
print("X has", X.shape[0], "rows and", X.shape[1], "columns")
for question, y in [("species", species), ("weight", weight)]:
    kind = "regression" if y.dtype.kind == "f" else "classification"
    print(f"{question:8s} y = {y}  ->  {kind}")
X has 3 rows and 2 columns
species  y = ['bamboo' 'spadenose' 'hammerhead']  ->  classification
weight   y = [0.281 0.228 2.61 ]  ->  regression

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If a model scores suspiciously well, look for an input that is a copy of the label or built from it. In this made-up table, girth was computed from weight, so girth nearly gives the weight away. Names such as tag numbers can leak in other ways. A4 treats leaks in detail.

Where this is used

Used in: A2 (a number as the label) and A3 (a category as the label). The grading of a model on sharks it has not seen is the subject of A4.

More questions

A model keeps learning from the sharks it sees at the dock, after training is finished. True or false?

False for the models of this primer. After training, the parameters stay fixed. The model reads them and does not change them. Learning happens again only when someone runs training on new labelled examples. C3 covers methods that adapt during use as a special case.

The lazy model

Guess first. The made-up table has 600 sharks: 268 spadenose, 200 milk sharks, 72 bamboo sharks, 57 hammerheads and 3 Ganges sharks. How often is a model right if it ignores the shark and always says the best single species? And can the month of the catch help a rule do better?

A baseline is a simple model that a complicated model must beat before we trust it. The lazy model is the baseline that ignores the inputs and always gives the most common label, or the average when the label is a number. On these records it always says spadenose and is right for 268 of 600 sharks, so the score to beat is an accuracy (the share of predictions that are right) of 44.7%. A model is worth keeping only if it beats this score on a measure that fits the purpose.

  1. Choose length as the input and drag the coral cut-off, a value that splits the sharks into two parts. Then choose the species the rule says for the short part and for the long part. Solid bars are right predictions and faded bars are mistakes.
  2. Aim to beat 44.7% and reach 70% accuracy with one cut-off, then press “Show the best rule for this input” to compare. Next choose the month as the input and try to beat 44.7% again.

One cut-off on length beats the score of 44.7% and reaches about 74% on these 600 sharks, but no cut-off on the month beats it.

How it works

Take a cut-off near 55 cm on length. Below it 258 sharks are spadenose, the most common species there, and above it 184 are milk sharks. A rule that says spadenose below and milk shark above is right for 258 + 184 = 442 of 600 sharks, which beats the score to beat.

accuracyof the rule: 73.7%=442right: 258 + 184÷600mvsscore to beat268 ÷ 600 = 44.7%

The score to beat is the base rate of the most common label (base rates in Part 0), the share of examples that have it. It depends on the data and not on the model, so in a table with 90% spadenose it would be 90%. The month does not help because spadenose is the most common species in all months with landings, so a rule on the month says spadenose and scores the same.

Common belief. A model that is right 74% of the time is a good model.

Why it fails. Whether 74% is good depends on the score to beat, because it is a large gain over 44.7% and falls below 90%. A score can also hide what matters. In a published table of 768 women (the Pima data), 268 have diabetes, so saying “no diabetes” to all women is right for 500 of 768 (65.1%). It finds none of the 268, which is useless for screening, the early testing for a disease.

Better account. Report a score next to the score to beat, on the same data, and read the gap.

Quick quiz

A table has 1,000 sharks and 620 of them are adults. What is the score to beat when a model predicts adult or juvenile?

It is the lazy model's 62%, because it always says “adult”. A model with 65% accuracy has barely beaten it.

In the Pima data, 268 of 768 women have diabetes. What is the score to beat, and what is wrong with the lazy model as a screening tool?

The lazy model says “no diabetes” for all women, so the score to beat is \(500/768 = 65.1\%\). It never finds a woman who has diabetes, although its accuracy looks respectable.

How the best-rule button works

The button “Show the best rule for this input” searches many cut-offs and shows the best one it finds, so use it after you have tried.

For a cut-off on length, say the commonest species on the two sides and count the sharks this gets right. Then move the cut-off and count again. At 30 cm both sides have spadenose as the commonest species, so the rule repeats the lazy model. As the cut-off moves right, the long side turns into mostly milk sharks while the short side stays spadenose, and the count peaks near 55 cm. After that it falls, because milk sharks start to fall on the short side (16 below 54.8 cm, 40 below 60 cm).

What the best rules never do

Notice what the best rules never do. None of them says "Ganges shark", because three sharks in 600 are too few to be the commonest species in any wide part. A4 returns to this: a model can score well and still miss the animal you care about.

A second baseline, from the clinic

In the published Pima data, 268 of 768 women have diabetes. The lazy model says "no diabetes" for all of them, so it scores:

500right: the women without diabetes÷768women in the table=65.1%lazy accuracy→0 of 268women with diabetes found

A screening model must also find women who have diabetes, so beating 65.1% is not enough. The sharks give the same warning: "no Ganges shark" is right for 597 of 600 records, 99.5%, and finds none of the three.

When it misleads

The baseline depends on how the labels are spread, so it changes from table to table. It also ignores cost. When missing a case is worse than a false alarm, a lazy model with a high score can be useless.

In practice

Keep a ladder of baselines: the lazy model, a one-cut rule, then the method in use today. Beat the highest rung that is cheap to run, and score all of them on the same sharks.

Symbols

\[ \text{accuracy} = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m} \mathbf{1}\bigl[\hat y^{(i)} = y^{(i)}\bigr] \qquad \text{lazy accuracy} = \frac{\max_k n_k}{m} \]

  • \(\mathbf{1}[\cdot]\) is 1 when the statement inside is true and 0 when it is false, so the sum counts the correct predictions.
  • \(n_k\) is the number of examples with label \(k\). The largest \(n_k\) over \(m\) is the base rate of the commonest label: \(268/600 = 0.447\).

In Python

import numpy as np

species = ["spadenose", "milk", "bamboo", "hammerhead", "ganges"]
# how many of the 600 made-up sharks fall below and above a 54.8 cm cut-off
below = np.array([258, 16, 57, 13, 0])
above = np.array([10, 184, 15, 44, 3])
total = below.sum() + above.sum()

lazy = (below + above).max() / total
rule = (below.max() + above.max()) / total
print("lazy model:", round(lazy, 3), "- always says", species[(below + above).argmax()])
print("one-cut rule:", round(rule, 3), "- says", species[below.argmax()], "below and", species[above.argmax()], "above")
lazy model: 0.447 - always says spadenose
one-cut rule: 0.737 - says spadenose below and milk above
import numpy as np

total = np.array([268, 200, 72, 57, 3])               # sharks per species in the made-up table
cuts = [30, 40, 45, 50, 54.8, 60, 70]                 # cut-offs on length, cm
# sharks shorter than each cut-off: one row per species (spadenose, milk, bamboo, hammerhead, Ganges)
below = np.array([[40, 148, 194, 237, 258, 268, 268],
                  [0, 0, 0, 3, 16, 40, 134],
                  [2, 15, 32, 49, 57, 62, 72],
                  [0, 2, 3, 5, 13, 16, 29],
                  [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]])

for j, cut in enumerate(cuts):
    right = below[:, j].max() + (total - below[:, j]).max()   # commonest species on each side
    print(f"cut at {cut:4.1f} cm: {right} of 600 right = {right / 600:.1%}")
cut at 30.0 cm: 268 of 600 right = 44.7%
cut at 40.0 cm: 348 of 600 right = 58.0%
cut at 45.0 cm: 394 of 600 right = 65.7%
cut at 50.0 cm: 434 of 600 right = 72.3%
cut at 54.8 cm: 442 of 600 right = 73.7%
cut at 60.0 cm: 428 of 600 right = 71.3%
cut at 70.0 cm: 334 of 600 right = 55.7%

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Before you celebrate a score, compute the lazy model's score on the same data. If your model is within a few points of it, the model has learned little. If it is far above and surprises you, look for a leak (A4).

Where this is used

Used in: a baseline is the first row of any results table (0.8). It is the starting point for grading in A4 and the first step of Karpathy's recipe for debugging networks (B8).

More questions

Your rule scores 74%, but you tuned its cut-off on the same 600 sharks you score it on. Should you trust the 74% for new sharks?

Treat it as optimistic. A rule tuned on the records can fit them a little better than it will fit new ones. Grading on records the rule never saw is the subject of A4.

Learning as a search for good dials

Guess first. The cube rule has one dial, so trying a few hundred settings is quick. A small neural network has thousands of dials. Suppose you try 10 settings of a dial, and a computer can test a million combinations per second. How long does a model with 20 dials take?

The loss is one number that says how badly a model does on the examples, and lower is better. In training, also called fitting, an algorithm searches for parameter values with a low loss, ideally the lowest. Testing settings resembles opening a combination lock: d dials of k settings give kd combinations (all the dials set together), as d wheels of k positions do. A random search tries settings at random and keeps the best. With many dials the combinations are too many to test, and random tries cover a vanishing share of them, so a smarter search is needed.

  1. The loss here is the average miss of the cube rule on 268 made-up spadenose sharks. Coral dots are tries and the teal ring marks the best so far. Press “Try 10”, then “Try 10 near the best so far”: the best so far moves to about a = 3.2.
  2. Press “Show the whole curve” to see the lowest point, about a = 3.3. Then set “Number of dials d” to 20, a lock with 20 wheels, and read the time to test all combinations.
Settings tried: 0Best so far: none yet

A few random tries, then tries near the best, find a good setting of one dial, but testing all combinations of 20 dials would take about 3 million years.

How it works

Take d = 20 dials (here d counts dials, not inputs) of k = 10 settings, a lock with 20 wheels. The number of combinations to test is kd = 1020. At 106 tests per second the search takes 1014 seconds, and a year has 3.16 × 107 seconds.

kd = 1020combinations: d = 20 dials, k = 10 settings÷106tests per second=1014 sseconds in all→1014 ÷ (3.16×107) = 3.2 millionyears: 1014 ÷ 107 = 107, then ÷ 3.16

Four more dials multiply the combinations by 10,000, to 3.2 × 1010 years for 24 dials. This is longer than the age of the universe, about 14 billion years. A lock gives no hint until it opens, but the loss can be computed at any setting we try. So many searches that make training practical use the slope of the loss: try a tiny turn of a dial up and down, and keep the direction in which the loss falls. The linear regression chapter builds the first such search, gradient descent.

Common belief. A deployed model keeps learning from the sharks it sees.

Why it fails. Using a model reads the settings of its dials, as looking at a lock reads its wheels, and leaves them alone. Training turns them, and training is a separate step with labelled examples.

Better account. Training and use are two phases. A model that changes during use needs a method built for it (the domain shift chapter covers one).

Quick quiz

You try 100 settings for 5 dials, a lock with 5 wheels. How many combinations is that?

\(100^5 = 10^{10}\), ten billion. At a million per second that is about 3 hours.

You try only 3 settings for 20 dials, a lock with 20 wheels. How many combinations is that, and how long at a million per second?

\(3^{20} = 3{,}486{,}784{,}401\) combinations, which take about 3,487 seconds, a little under an hour. With 30 dials the same grid would take over six years.

Go deeper a search you can run, symbols, Python about 4 min

How the figure searches

A press of “Try one random a” tests one setting and plots it. The curve is hidden at first, because an actual search sees only the points it has tried. “Try 10 near the best so far” zooms in. That is a search with two stages, wide and then narrow, and it works well for one dial. “Show the whole curve” lets you check your best against the true lowest point.

Symbols

\[ \text{combinations} = k^{d} \qquad\qquad \theta^{\star} = \arg\min_{\theta}\; L(\theta) \]

  • \(k\) is the number of settings tried per dial and \(d\) is the number of dials.
  • \(L(\theta)\) is the loss for the parameters \(\theta\) (A2 gives the standard formula). \(\arg\min\) means "the argument that gives the smallest value", so \(\theta^{\star}\) is the best setting of the dials.

A search you can run

The code below repeats the two stages of the figure on the eight records, with a fixed seed. The best of five wide tries has an average miss of 0.040 kg. Five more tries within one millionth of it find 3.15 millionths and 0.017 kg. The grid of the first code block, with 801 settings, reaches 0.015 kg.

When it breaks

The loss curve of one dial is a single valley, so narrowing the range around the best try makes sense. With several valleys the second stage could settle in the wrong one. A try also reveals only the loss at that setting, not which way is downhill. Gradient descent adds that missing piece, the slope.

In practice

Random search is a common way to set hyperparameters, the settings chosen before training such as a learning rate, with a few dozen tries. Draw a dial that spans orders of magnitude on a log scale: pick the exponent at random, then raise 10 to it. On a linear scale from \(10^{-7}\) to \(10^{-4}\), nine tries in ten exceed \(10^{-5}\).

In Python

import numpy as np

length = np.array([18.2, 29.2, 33.2, 36.5, 39.4, 42.8, 46.4, 51.3])
weight = np.array([0.018, 0.066, 0.128, 0.169, 0.167, 0.287, 0.297, 0.413])

settings = np.linspace(0, 8e-6, 801)          # 801 settings of the dial a
miss = [np.abs(a * length ** 3 - weight).mean() for a in settings]
best = settings[int(np.argmin(miss))]
print(f"best of 801 settings: a = {best:.2e}, average miss = {min(miss):.3f} kg")
print("settings to try with 20 dials at 10 settings each:", 10 ** 20)
best of 801 settings: a = 3.06e-06, average miss = 0.015 kg
settings to try with 20 dials at 10 settings each: 100000000000000000000
import numpy as np

length = np.array([18.2, 29.2, 33.2, 36.5, 39.4, 42.8, 46.4, 51.3])
weight = np.array([0.018, 0.066, 0.128, 0.169, 0.167, 0.287, 0.297, 0.413])
miss = lambda a: np.abs(a * length ** 3 - weight).mean()

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
wide = rng.uniform(0, 8e-6, 5)                      # stage 1: five tries anywhere in 0 to 8 millionths
for a in wide:
    print(f"wide  a = {a:.2e}  average miss = {miss(a):.3f}")
best = wide[np.argmin([miss(a) for a in wide])]
near = rng.uniform(best - 1e-6, best + 1e-6, 5)     # stage 2: five tries within 1 millionth of the best
for a in near:
    print(f"near  a = {a:.2e}  average miss = {miss(a):.3f}")
both = np.r_[wide, near]
top = both[np.argmin([miss(a) for a in both])]
print(f"best of 10 tries: a = {top:.2e}, average miss = {miss(top):.3f} kg")
wide  a = 4.09e-06  average miss = 0.058
wide  a = 7.60e-06  average miss = 0.273
wide  a = 1.15e-06  average miss = 0.122
wide  a = 7.59e-06  average miss = 0.272
wide  a = 2.49e-06  average miss = 0.040
near  a = 2.34e-06  average miss = 0.050
near  a = 3.15e-06  average miss = 0.017
near  a = 2.31e-06  average miss = 0.051
near  a = 2.59e-06  average miss = 0.034
near  a = 1.55e-06  average miss = 0.098
best of 10 tries: a = 3.15e-06, average miss = 0.017 kg

Common mistakes

Debug tip. When you search, look at where the best value falls. If it falls at the edge of the range you tried, the true best may lie outside it, so widen the range.

Where this is used

Used in: gradient descent (A2), the loss of a network (B3) and the many-dial searches of B5.

More questions

Your best setting of a dial is the largest value you tried. What do you do?

Try larger values. The true best may lie beyond the edge of the range.

Exercises

Theory

  1. theory A table has 1,000 sharks and 620 are adults. What accuracy does the lazy model score for adult or juvenile? A second table has 1,000 sharks and 50 of one rare species. What does the lazy model score for "is it this rare species", and what does that say about quoting accuracy alone?

    Hint

    The lazy model says the commonest label. Count the sharks it gets right.

  2. theory How many parameters do these models have? (a) \(\hat y = a L^3\). (b) \(\hat y = w x + b\). (c) \(\hat y = w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + w_3 x_3 + b\). (d) \(\hat y = a L^{k}\), where both \(a\) and \(k\) are dials. Which of these have the same form but different numbers of parameters?

  3. theory Explain in two or three sentences why the tag number should not be an input to a species model. What would happen to a new shark's tag?

Practice

  1. practice Load catch.csv with pandas. Compute the lazy model's accuracy for the column mature on all 600 records. Then compute the accuracy of the rule "mature if length is at least 40 cm" and compare.

  2. practice For the spadenose records only, search settings of \(a\) in \(\hat y = a L^3\) from 1e-6 to 8e-6 and report the setting with the smallest average miss. How far is it from 3.3e-6, and why might it differ?

  3. practice Build the best one-cut rule for the species using the weight instead of the length. Report the cut-off, the two species it says and the accuracy.

    Hint

    Try all the midpoints between sorted weights, and in the two parts say the commonest species.

Think deeper

  1. open SharkCam looks at 2,400 video frames from one dive. Suppose a shark is in view in 199 of them. What is the lazy model for "is a shark in view", and what does it score? What would you want to know about a detector besides its accuracy?

  2. open A teammate says: "My rule gets 74%, so it has understood what separates the species." How would you test the claim? Which simpler explanations would you rule out first?

  3. open Name two inputs SharkCam has on the boat at the dock that it would not have on a dive. How would that change what a model trained on dock records can do underwater?

Come back later

Try these after two days and again after a week, without looking back.

A shark is twice as long as another. The cube rule predicts how many times the weight? (0.3) And what does the dial \(a\) do to that ratio?

Eight times, since \(2^3 = 8\). The dial \(a\) cancels in the ratio: it scales all predictions together and leaves the ratio alone.

A bar chart shows a model's accuracy as 74% next to a bar for the lazy model, and the axis starts at 40%. What are two things to check? (0.8)

Check that the axis starts at zero, because a truncated axis makes a gap look bigger. Check that both bars are scored on the same data. The gap between 74% and 44.7% is large on a fair axis too, but its size depends on the baseline.

The average of the nine spadenose lengths in 0.7 is 37.2 cm. If your model had no inputs, would it predict this value for a shark's length? Why is that the lazy model for a number?

Yes. With no inputs, a model for a number can say only one thing for all sharks, and the mean is the single value with the smallest squared miss (A2). That is the lazy model for numbers.
